Most revenue reporting problems are not hard SQL. They’re the same handful of problems showing up in different tables: gaps in the calendar, days cut at the wrong midnight, duplicate records, totals that need a comparison, data that quietly stopped arriving, and two systems that disagree about the same month. I’ve settled on a small set of Snowflake patterns for them. Here they are, with generic table names. Swap in your own.
If a day had no orders, a plain GROUP BY leaves it out and the chart skips the day as if it never happened. Generate the calendar first and left join the facts onto it, so a quiet day shows up as zero instead of vanishing. If you already have a dim_date table, join to that instead of the generator. SEQ4 can have gaps, so use ROW_NUMBER for the offset.

I implemented Raft from the paper in Go — leader election, log replication, snapshotting, joint-consensus membership changes — with a linearizable key/value store on top.
The difficult part wasn't implementing the happy path. It was finding the defects that only became reachable once log compaction removed the redundancy that had been hiding them.
Adding snapshotting exposed three real bugs. A deterministic simulator I had built beforehand caught the subtlest one and pinned it to a single seed — seed 188 — which then reproduced it exactly throughout the diagnosis. The other two were caught by a storage conformance suite and a restart test. This post walks through each one, from trigger to regression test, along with the false positive I refused to count.

articles.author: Krish Khati
articles.description:
At 2:17 am, the terminal screamed “permission denied” as I tried to push the live‑publish branch to the staging server. I stared at the error, then at the diff that added a tiny wrapper around the model’s output to run a basic quality check before sending it to the web. The commit was meant to be a safety net, a single line that would block obviously malformed responses. In practice it felt like a Band‑Aid on a wound that keeps bleeding.
I spent the next hour replaying the same request through the new gate, watching the check reject a perfectly valid answer because a stray newline tripped the length filter. That made me realize I had been too eager to call the feature “ready”. My opinion is simple: a quality check is only useful if you understand the failure modes, not if you assume the check itself is flawless.
The bug forced me to step back and redesign the validation logic, separating syntactic sanity from semantic relevance. I also learned that “basic” in a commit message can be a dangerous understatement; it encouraged me to skip a proper test suite for the new path.
Now the live‑publish endpoint refuses to serve anything that doesn’t pass the new filter, and I finally have a reproducible failure to write a test for. The night ended with a quiet terminal and a reminder that shortcuts rarely survive real traffic.
articles.title: Late‑night push and the illusion of good enough

Topics are partitioned, meaning each topic can have multiple partitions to allow parallel processing.
Example: A topic named user_activity could store logs of user actions on a website.

Each topic is divided into partitions, which are ordered, immutable sequences of records.
